agent_notes: The sources attach several different referents to the enemies (Titus in Rashi, Gog and Magog in Radak and Meiri, Amalek at v11). I did not choose between these and describe only what the Hebrew says.

שֶׁכֶם (shekhem) is literally 'shoulder'. The five English versions split: KJV, ASV, Webster and BBE read 'turn the back' (cf. Ex 23:27); YLT reads 'a butt', a target. The medieval commentators go another way: Rashi (a portion, the spoil Israel divides), Ibn Ezra (one band, joined together), Radak ('one portion, all of them'), Meiri ('one portion before you'), Metzudat David (set apart in one corner as a target for the arrow), Metzudat Zion (portion, as in Gen 48:22) and Malbim (a measuring line, tied to 2 Sam 8:2) all read 'portion' or 'one'; the Targum has 'one shoulder'. I keep 'shoulder' in the literal layer and the glosses, and the dramatic layer follows the 'turn the back' reading, against the medieval commentators; the commentary says so. Ibn Ezra adds that the accent (etnachta) falls on shekhem, so it pairs with 'one', as in shekhem echad.

STEPBible glosses מֵיתָרֶיךָ as 'bowstrings'; the literal sense is 'your cords/strings'. The verb תְּכוֹנֵן has no stated object: the arrows are understood (Ibn Ezra, Radak both call this an ellipsis). I put the supplied object in brackets in the literal layer.
